blocks.heading: Propositional logic
blocks.text: Propositional logic studies statements and how logical connectives combine them into compound statements. The truth of a compound statement depends on its parts and its connectives.

blocks.heading: Discrete mathematics
blocks.text: Discrete mathematics studies distinct structures such as integers, sets, logical statements, functions, algorithms, graphs, and combinatorics. Logic provides tools for checking arguments and proofs.

blocks.heading: Discrete and continuous
blocks.text: A count of coins is discrete: it changes in whole-number steps. Time, height, temperature, and length are commonly modeled as continuous quantities.

blocks.heading: Propositions
blocks.text: A proposition is a declarative statement with exactly one truth value: true or false. “2 + 2 = 4” is true. “2 + 2 = 5” is false. Commands such as “Go home” and questions such as “Are you okay?” are not propositions.

blocks.heading: Logical connectives
blocks.text: A logical connective combines or modifies propositions. ¬ means NOT; ∧ means AND; ∨ means inclusive OR; ⊕ means exclusive OR; → means IF … THEN; ↔ means IF AND ONLY IF.

blocks.heading: Negation
blocks.text: Negation reverses a truth value. We write ¬p or ~p. If p is true, ¬p is false, and conversely. p: It is raining. ¬p: It is not raining. Negating “I will not study” gives “I will study.”

blocks.heading: Conjunction
blocks.text: A conjunction, p ∧ q, is true only when both propositions are true. p: The sky is blue. q: The grass is green. p ∧ q: The sky is blue and the grass is green.

blocks.heading: Disjunction
blocks.text: An inclusive disjunction, p ∨ q, is true when at least one proposition is true, including when both are true. It is false only when both are false. p ∨ q: It is raining or it is snowing, or both.

blocks.heading: Exclusive OR
blocks.text: Exclusive OR, p ⊕ q, is true when exactly one proposition is true. It is false when both truth values match. “I will eat either a burger or fries, but not both” expresses exclusive OR.

blocks.heading: Implication
blocks.text: A conditional, p → q, means “if p, then q.” Here p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. It is false only when p is true and q is false. p: I study. q: I pass. p → q: If I study, then I pass.

blocks.heading: Biconditional
blocks.text: A biconditional, p ↔ q, means “p if and only if q.” It is true when p and q have the same truth value. It asserts both p → q and q → p. p ↔ q: You can access the system if and only if you have a password.

blocks.heading: Connective reference
blocks.text: ¬p: reverses p. p ∧ q: both true. p ∨ q: at least one true. p ⊕ q: exactly one true. p → q: false only for true → false. p ↔ q: matching truth values.
